title: the Pandavas' last journey, Yudhishthira's dog, heaven
hook: the kingdom is handed on, the brothers and Draupadi take off their ornaments and walk out of the city, and a dog follows them
tomorrow: the Pandavas' last journey, Yudhishthira's dog, heaven

segments.voice: Yesterday closed Ashvamedhika with a half-golden mongoose and a family's handful of flour. Between that book and today's, the epic tells of the elders' deaths in the forest and the end of Krishna's people. Your line was a handful of barley. Day eight hundred seventy-three.

The news from Dwaraka reaches Hastinapura: Krishna is gone, and his clan has destroyed itself. Yudhishthira hears it and makes up his mind in one sentence, in Ganguli's telling: time is cooking all creatures. It's time to go. He crowns Parikshit, the child who was born without breath, now grown. He puts the kingdom in others' care. Then the five brothers and Draupadi take off their jewelry, put on the plain clothes of forest hermits, and walk out through the gates. The city follows them a little way, weeping, and turns back. One companion does not turn back. A dog.
screen: `NEWS FROM DWARAKA.` → `PARIKSHIT IS CROWNED.` → `SIX WALK OUT, AND A DOG.`

segments.voice: This book is called the Mahaprasthanika, the book of the great departure, and it has the feel of a last chapter. The Pandavas walk east first. Yudhishthira leads, then Bhima, then Arjuna, then the twins, then Draupadi, and the dog behind them all. They reach the sea. And there, a figure stands in their path, tall as a mountain: Agni, the god of fire. He speaks to Arjuna. Remember the great bow Gandiva? Agni himself brought it to Arjuna, long ago, from Varuna, the lord of the waters. Now Agni asks for it back. Its work is finished, he says. It belongs to Varuna; give it to the sea. And Arjuna, who has carried that bow through the whole war, throws it into the waves, along with his quivers that never ran empty. Arjuna the archer walks on unarmed. This is how the great departure starts: not with a battle or a prayer, but with letting go of the thing you were best known for. The ornaments come off at the gate. The bow goes into the sea. The kingdom is in Parikshit's hands. Each step is lighter. And then the walk itself begins, around the edge of the world: south, then west, where they see the sea over the place Dwaraka stood, then north, toward the mountains. They are walking toward Meru, toward heaven, in their bodies, while they still have them. And the dog keeps coming.
screen: `MAHAPRASTHANIKA: THE GREAT DEPARTURE` · `AGNI STANDS AT THE SEA` · `"GIVE GANDIVA BACK TO VARUNA"` · then, large: `THE BOW GOES INTO THE WAVES`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably, and let your hands rest empty. Bring to mind one thing you're known for, a skill, a role, a title, something that has carried you a long way. Breathe in and thank it, quietly, for its work. Breathe out and imagine setting it down beside you, just for these two minutes. Notice what's left when it's not in your hands. If you pray, you can rest in your prayer without it. The bell holds the time.
Mahaprasthanika. The book of the great departure: five brothers, Draupadi and a dog walk out of the city, and Arjuna gives his bow back to the sea.
Your line: each step is lighter. Today, put down one thing you usually carry, a phone, a role, a habit, for an hour, and walk on without it. Day eight hundred seventy-three.

howItsDone: The Mahaprasthanika Parva tells the Pandavas' final walk; Hindus hear it in recitations of the epic, and the image of the brothers, Draupadi and the dog walking toward the Himalayas is often painted and retold.

fork.setup: you're Arjuna, at the edge of the sea. the god of fire asks you to give back the bow that has made you who you are. what do you do?
options: keep it; you may still need it.
fork.reveal: Arjuna throws Gandiva and his quivers into the water, returning them to Varuna, and walks on.

original.note: mahaprasthanika: the name of the book of the great departure.

trapdoor: what you thought: the last journey is a march to heaven.
what it means: it begins with giving things up: ornaments, a kingdom, and Arjuna's bow.
what a scholar hears: the bow came from Varuna through Agni, so throwing it in the sea returns it to its owner.

notes: All paraphrase. The serial passes from Ashvamedhika to Mahaprasthanika; the review mentions the intervening books (Ashramavasika, Mausala) in one line. A Keeper may wish to add a bridge day.
"Time is cooking all creatures" is a paraphrase of Yudhishthira's words in Ganguli; confirm the sense.
Confirm who was entrusted with the kingdom (Parikshit crowned; Yuyutsu and others given charge) and left general here.
Confirm the walking order (Yudhishthira, Bhima, Arjuna, the twins, Draupadi, the dog) and the direction of the circuit (east, south, west seeing Dwaraka submerged, north).
Superlatives and length claims were removed under the claims rule.
Editor pass: 'every battle of this serial' softened to 'the whole war'.
Audit (serious): removed 'young Parikshit' / 'a boy's hands'. The departure comes thirty-six years after the war (Mausala Parva), so Parikshit is a grown man when crowned, not a boy.
